items.stem: Gravity is best described as a force that...

options.text: Always pulls objects with mass toward each other
Pushes objects with mass away from each other
Pulls some objects and pushes others, depending on their charge
Acts only on metal objects, like a magnet

items.explanation: Gravity is always an attractive force. It only ever pulls objects that have mass toward each other, and it never pushes them apart.

items.stem: How does an object's mass affect the strength of its gravitational pull?

options.text: More mass makes the gravitational pull weaker
Mass changes the direction of gravity but not its strength
More mass makes the gravitational pull stronger
Mass has no effect on gravity at all

items.explanation: More mass means a stronger gravitational pull. That is why the giant objects in the universe, planets, moons, and stars, are the ones whose gravity we notice.

items.stem: Two students stand close together. Do they attract each other through gravity?

options.text: No, gravity only works between objects in outer space
Yes, but the pull is far too weak to feel because their masses are small
No, people do not have any mass for gravity to act on
Yes, and they are pulled together hard enough to feel it

items.explanation: Every object with mass attracts every other object with mass, so the two students do pull on each other. But because their masses are tiny, the force is far too weak to feel.

items.stem: Why do you feel a pull toward Earth but not toward a parked car right next to you?

options.text: Earth is closer to you than the car is
The car is made of metal, which blocks gravity
Only Earth has gravity; the car has none
Earth's mass is enormous, while the car's mass is far too small to produce a pull you can feel

items.explanation: Gravity becomes noticeable only when at least one object has a very large mass. Earth's mass is enormous, so you feel its pull. The car's mass is far too small to notice.

items.stem: Which observation is the best evidence that gravity is an attractive force?

options.text: A magnet picking up paper clips
A balloon sticking to a wall after you rub it
A dropped ball always falling toward the ground, never upward
A compass needle pointing north

items.explanation: A dropped object always falls toward Earth, never away from it. We have never seen gravity push something away, which is strong evidence that gravity only pulls.

items.stem: An astronaut weighs less on the Moon than on Earth. What is the best explanation?

options.text: The Moon has less mass than Earth, so its gravitational pull is weaker
There is no gravity on the Moon, so weight disappears
The astronaut's mass shrinks while on the Moon
The Moon pushes the astronaut upward

items.explanation: The Moon has much less mass than Earth, so it pulls with only about 1/6 the strength. The astronaut's mass stays the same; only the weight changes because the pull is weaker.

items.stem: Earth's gravity constantly pulls the Moon. Why doesn't the Moon crash into Earth?

options.text: Earth's gravity does not reach all the way to the Moon
The Moon moves sideways fast enough that it keeps falling around Earth instead of into it
The Moon's gravity cancels out Earth's gravity
There is no gravity in space to pull the Moon in

items.explanation: The Moon is always falling toward Earth, but it is also moving sideways very fast. Earth curves away beneath it at the same rate, so it keeps falling around Earth. That is an orbit.

options.text: the two objects are touching each other
the objects are made of the same material
the objects are electrically charged
at least one object has a very large mass

items.explanation: Gravity acts between all objects with mass, but you only notice it when at least one object is very massive, like a planet, moon, or star.

items.stem: Ocean tides on Earth are caused mainly by...

options.text: the Moon's gravity pulling on Earth's water
the Sun heating the ocean during the day
Earth's magnetic field pushing the water
wind pushing waves toward the shore

items.explanation: Tides are caused mainly by the Moon's gravity tugging on Earth's water. The fact that the Moon can move whole oceans from 240,000 miles away is evidence that large masses pull hard.

items.stem: A student claims, 'Gravity can push two objects apart.' Which evidence best argues against this claim?

options.text: Heavier objects are harder to lift off the ground
Astronauts float around inside a spaceship
Objects released above the ground always fall down toward Earth, never away from it
The Moon stays in orbit around Earth

items.explanation: If gravity could push, we would sometimes see objects fly away when released. Instead, dropped objects always fall toward Earth. That consistent evidence shows gravity only pulls.
